mcqs.question: A background task does almost no CPU work but sends a tiny 200-byte network request every 30 seconds. Why might this drain more battery than an occasional heavy CPU computation?
options: Small network payloads always require more CPU to serialize than large ones
The OS charges a fixed CPU penalty for any network-related system call
The radio's ramp-up and tail cost is paid on every wakeup regardless of payload size, so frequent small requests rack up that fixed cost repeatedly, unlike a single CPU burst
Network requests always run at maximum CPU priority
mcqs.explanation: The radio's ramp-up/tail cost is largely fixed per active period, so many small, frequent requests pay that fixed cost over and over, often outweighing an occasional CPU-heavy but network-free task. Payload size and CPU serialization cost are minor compared to that fixed radio cost.

mcqs.question: Why can't an app simply spawn a background thread and expect it to keep running indefinitely once the app is backgrounded?
options: Background threads are technically disabled at the OS level
Threads are automatically converted into foreground services
Only single-threaded apps are allowed to run in the background
Background execution is a privilege the OS grants and can revoke; sustained background work must go through OS-mediated scheduling APIs it can throttle or defer
mcqs.explanation: Both platforms treat background execution as something the OS actively manages and can suspend or kill, not a guarantee an app controls on its own — which is exactly why sustained background work has to go through scheduling APIs the OS can batch, defer, or deny. Threads aren't disabled; they're simply not exempt from OS-level suspension.

mcqs.question: A wakelock is acquired before a network call and released only inside the success callback. What's the risk?
options: The wakelock automatically expires after 60 seconds regardless of code path
If the call hangs, errors, or the response never arrives, the wakelock is never released and the device stays fully awake, draining battery indefinitely
Nothing — wakelocks only affect screen brightness, not CPU power
The OS will silently ignore wakelocks held longer than a few seconds
mcqs.explanation: Without a guaranteed release on error/timeout paths and an explicit backstop timeout, a stuck or lost network call leaves the wakelock held indefinitely, keeping the device fully awake — a classic "phone died overnight" cause. Wakelocks don't auto-expire and directly affect CPU sleep state, not screen brightness.

mcqs.question: A nightly analytics batch upload is implemented to run immediately the moment data is generated, insisting on network access right away. What's wrong with this classification?
options: Analytics uploads should never be sent from mobile clients at all
This is deferrable maintenance work being treated as urgent, wasting battery on immediate execution for data nobody is waiting on, when it should run on a scheduled job with loose constraints
The upload should instead be classified as user-facing, time-sensitive work
There's nothing wrong; all network requests should run immediately for reliability
mcqs.explanation: Analytics data has no user waiting on it, so it's a textbook case of deferrable maintenance work — scheduling it with loose constraints (charging, WiFi, a flexible window) lets the OS batch it efficiently instead of paying a dedicated radio wakeup for each immediate upload.

mcqs.question: An app polls the server every 15 seconds to check for new messages, even when the user is inactive for hours. What's the better architecture?
options: Push notifications or a persistent connection that wakes the client only when something actually changes, instead of paying a fixed radio cost on a tight independent timer
Reduce the interval to every 5 seconds for faster updates
Keep polling every 15 seconds but only when the screen is on
Move the polling logic to run entirely on a background thread
mcqs.explanation: Push-based delivery only wakes the client when there's genuinely new data, so idle periods cost nothing — a tight independent poll pays the radio's fixed wakeup cost every interval regardless of activity. Polling faster or moving it to a thread makes the underlying problem worse or irrelevant, not better.

mcqs.question: Why is 'my phone died overnight for no reason' a classic symptom of a wakelock bug rather than a doze/standby issue?
options: Doze mode and app standby are designed to prevent exactly this by suspending background apps, so a battery drain that bypasses them usually means an app is actively holding the device awake via an unreleased wakelock
Doze mode only activates during the day, so overnight drains are unrelated to it
It's always caused by a corrupted battery calibration file
Overnight drains can only be caused by a malfunctioning charging cable
mcqs.explanation: Doze and standby exist specifically to stop background apps from draining battery while idle overnight, so when a drain happens anyway, the most common cause is an app actively holding a wakelock that's preventing the device from ever truly sleeping — a mechanism explicitly designed to bypass those very protections.
